analogy.p: Imagine a box of index cards for a school library. Each card is a record: it has the same printed boxes on it (title, author, year, shelf), and those boxes are the fields. The whole box is the table. An SQL query is like asking the librarian: 'SELECT the title and shelf FROM the box WHERE the author starts with T'. She flips through every card, ignores the ones that do not match, and hands you a fresh list with only the boxes you asked for. This maps correctly because the cards never change; you only get a filtered copy. It breaks down because a real database finds matches very quickly using indexes and can search millions of cards, whereas a human librarian would have to check them one by one.
analogy.t: A filing cabinet of index cards

bullets: A record = a collection of related **fields** that together describe **one entity** (one person, one item, one event).
Every record in the same set has the **same structure**: the same fields, in the same order, with the same data types.
Example record for one student: StudentID = 3, Name = "Chloe", Year = 11, Score = 65, Passed = True.
Records let a programmer pass around, store and search a whole 'row' of information instead of lots of loose variables, which keeps programs **organised and easier to maintain**.
The values differ from record to record, but the **field names** and **data types** stay the same for every record.
A record is **not** the same as an array: an array holds many items of the **same data type**, a record holds items that can be **different data types**.
core.p: A **record** is a data structure that stores a group of related items of data about one thing, such as one student, one product or one book. Each item inside the record is called a **field**, and the fields of one record all describe the same entity. Instead of keeping a student's ID, name, year group and score in four unrelated variables, you keep them together as a single unit so the program can treat them as one 'thing'. This is why records are used to store data in the structured way that databases and files rely on.

bullets: **Field** = one named piece of data in a record (one column of a table); **field name** = the label used to refer to it.
Typical data types by field: ID → integer; Name → string; Year → integer; Score → integer or real; Passed → Boolean.
Use an **integer** for whole numbers you may calculate with, a **string** for text (including phone numbers, which you never do arithmetic on), a **Boolean** for True/False.
Fields are referred to by name, for example student.Name, so code is easier to read than using index numbers.
Good field names are short, meaningful and consistent (Score, not x1), which links to **maintainability** in the robust-programs topic.
Choosing the wrong type causes errors: storing a score as a string means "9" sorts after "10" alphabetically and cannot be added up directly.
core.h: Fields, field names and data types
core.p: Each field in a record has a **field name** (an identifier such as Name or Score) and a **data type** (such as integer, string, real or Boolean) that decides what sort of value it can hold. Choosing the right data type matters because it controls how much memory is used, which operations are allowed and how the data can be validated. Because every record has the same fields, a program can write code like 'look at the Score field of every record' and know it will work for all of them.

bullets: **Table** = the whole set of records about one kind of thing (the Students table, the Products table).
**Row = record**; **column = field**. Learn this pairing exactly, it is a very common 1-mark question.
A **flat-file database** stores all its data in a **single table**, with no links to other tables.
Because each record is one row, adding a new item means **adding a new record** (a new row) to the table.
Tables can be stored in a file (for example a text/CSV file where each line is one record and commas separate the fields), linking to **file handling**.
A real database management system can then answer questions using **SQL**, rather than the programmer writing a loop to search every record.
core.p: A collection of records of the same type is stored as a **table**, and a simple database of one table is called a **flat-file database**. Picture a spreadsheet: each column is a field, each row is a record, and the whole grid is the table. The table has a name, such as Students, and that name is what an SQL query uses after the word FROM. Storing data like this means information can be saved to a file, searched and sorted far more easily than data scattered across the program.

bullets: Array: items share one data type, access by **index**, e.g. scores[2].
Record: items can have **different data types**, access by **field name**, e.g. student.Score.
**Array of records** = a list of students where each element is a whole student record; this is how a table is held in memory.
**Parallel arrays** (names[ ], scores[ ] with matching indexes) are an older workaround; they break if one array is sorted or edited and the others are not.
A 2D array forces everything to be the same type (often strings), so numbers must be **cast** before calculating.
Records make code more readable and reduce mistakes because each value is labelled by a meaningful field name.
core.h: Records compared with arrays and parallel arrays
core.p: Arrays and records both store several items, but they solve different problems. An **array** stores many values of the **same data type** under one name, accessed by an index, whereas a **record** stores several **different fields** about one thing. A 2D array can imitate a table of records, but every item must be the same data type and fields are found by column number rather than by name. Combining the two gives the usual real-world structure: an **array of records**, where each element of the array is one record.

bullets: **Add**: append a new record with a value for every field (for a file, write a new line).
**Read**: read a line from the file, split it at the delimiter (such as a comma) to get the fields, then cast numeric fields from string to integer/real.
**Edit**: find the record, change the field value, then save the updated data back (often by rewriting the file).
**Search**: loop through all records testing a condition, e.g. IF record.Score >= 60 THEN, or use SQL with WHERE.
Always **close the file** after reading or writing so data is saved and the file is released.
Check the data is **valid** before it is stored (range check on Score, presence check on Name) so the table does not fill with errors.
core.h: Working with records: adding, reading, editing and searching
core.p: Programs usually need four jobs done with records: create new ones, read them back, change them, and search for particular ones. When records are saved in a file, each record is normally read in as one line of text and split into its separate fields, then converted to the correct data types. Searching a flat file without a database means looping through every record and testing a condition, which is exactly what the WHERE clause of an SQL query does for you in one statement.

bullets: SQL = **Structured Query Language**; a **query** is a request for data from a database.
SQL is **declarative**: you state **what** you want, not step-by-step **how** to find it.
A basic query has the shape: SELECT (which fields) FROM (which table) WHERE (which records).
The query returns a **result set**, a new table containing only the fields and records requested; the original table is unchanged.
SQL keywords are conventionally written in **capital letters** (SELECT, FROM, WHERE); table and field names must be spelled exactly as in the database.
A statement is normally ended with a semicolon in many systems, but in OCR exam answers focus on getting the clauses and conditions right.
Searching with SQL is quicker to write and less error-prone than coding a loop to check every record.
core.h: What SQL is and why it is used
core.p: **SQL** stands for **Structured Query Language**. It is a language used to **search for and retrieve data** from a database, and the J277 specification focuses on the commands SELECT, FROM, WHERE, LIKE, AND and OR. Rather than writing loops, you describe what you want (which fields, from which table, matching which condition) and the database finds it. SQL is fast, standard across many systems and works well on very large amounts of data.

bullets: Pattern: **SELECT** field1, field2 **FROM** TableName.
Example: SELECT Name, Score FROM Students returns two columns (Name and Score) for all six students.
SELECT picks **columns (fields)**; WHERE (next) picks **rows (records)**. Do not mix these up.
The order of the fields in the result follows the order written after SELECT.
Fields are separated by **commas**, with no comma after the last field and none between SELECT and the first field.
FROM is always followed by the **table name**, not by a field name.
A misspelled field or table name makes the query fail; copy the names exactly from the question.
core.p: **SELECT** says which **fields** (columns) you want in the result, and **FROM** says which **table** to take them from. Together they let you pick out just the columns you need. Several fields are listed in the order you want them, separated by **commas**. With only SELECT and FROM and no WHERE, the query returns that field for **every record** in the table.

bullets: SELECT * FROM Students returns every field of every record (the whole table).
SELECT * FROM Students WHERE Year = 11 returns all fields, but only for Year 11 records.
* is a **wildcard for field names** in SELECT; do not confuse it with the % wildcard used inside LIKE patterns.
Use named fields instead of * when the question asks for specific fields (for example 'names only'), otherwise you may lose marks for extra data.
The result still has one row per matching record; the star affects columns, not rows.
core.p: Writing **SELECT \*** means 'select **all fields**'. It saves typing every field name and is useful when you want the complete record. The star only decides which columns appear; whether every record or only some come back is still controlled by WHERE. In an exam, use the star when the question says 'all the details', 'all the data' or 'everything' about the matching records.

bullets: Operators: **=** (equal to), **<>** or **!=** (not equal to), **<** (less than), **>** (greater than), **<=** (less than or equal), **>=** (greater than or equal).
In SQL a single **=** is used to **test equality** (unlike many programming languages that use ==).
Example: WHERE Score >= 60 includes a score of exactly 60; WHERE Score > 60 does **not**.
WHERE comes **after** FROM: SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Score >= 60.
The field in the condition does **not** have to be one of the fields in SELECT; you can filter on Score but display only Name.
If no record meets the condition, the result is **empty** (no rows), not an error.
Dates and numbers are compared by value; text is compared alphabetically (character codes).
core.p: **WHERE** filters the records so that only those meeting a **condition** are returned. The condition compares a field with a value using a comparison operator. WHERE is checked for each record in turn: if the condition is true the record is included, if false it is left out. Choosing the right operator is crucial, especially the difference between greater than and greater than or equal to.

bullets: Text: WHERE Name = 'Chloe' (quotes needed).
Number: WHERE Year = 11 (no quotes).
Match the value type to the field's **data type**: a string field gets a quoted value, an integer field gets a bare number.
Text matching in SQL compares the exact characters you give, so spell and punctuate the value as it appears in the data.
Forgetting quotes around text can make the database think you mean a field name, so the query fails or returns the wrong result.
Use quotes consistently: do not start with a single quote and finish with a double quote.
core.h: Writing text and number values in conditions
core.p: How you write the value matters. **Text (string) values are put in quotation marks**, such as 'Chloe' or "Chloe", whereas **numbers are written without quotes**. Exam questions accept either single or double quotes if used consistently. Boolean fields are usually compared with TRUE or FALSE depending on the system. A common error is forgetting the quotes round text or putting quotes round numbers.

bullets: **AND**: both conditions must be true. WHERE Year = 11 AND Score > 50.
**OR**: either (or both) conditions can be true. WHERE Year = 10 OR Score > 80.
Write each condition completely: WHERE Score > 40 AND Score < 70, not WHERE Score > 40 AND < 70.
AND narrows the results; OR widens them. Think 'and = both, or = either'.
A range check such as 'between 40 and 70' is written as Score >= 40 AND Score <= 70 (use the right inclusive/exclusive operators).
AND and OR can be combined, but at GCSE use them clearly; brackets can show which is worked out first.
The same logic idea appears in Boolean logic (AND/OR gates) and in IF statements, which is a good link to remember.
core.h: Combining conditions with AND and OR
core.p: **AND** and **OR** let one query test more than one condition. With **AND**, a record is returned only if **both** conditions are true; with **OR**, a record is returned if **at least one** is true. This means AND usually makes the result smaller (stricter) and OR usually makes it larger (more relaxed). Each condition must be written in full, with the field name repeated on both sides.

bullets: **Starts with**: LIKE 'S%' (Sam, Sara, Steve).
**Ends with**: LIKE '%son' (Jackson, Wilson).
**Contains**: LIKE '%an%' (Dan, Hannah, Bryan).
LIKE is used with **text values in quotes**; the pattern is a string.
% can stand for **zero, one or many** characters, so 'S%' also matches just 'S'.
= needs an exact match; LIKE with % allows a partial match. Use LIKE whenever the question says 'begins with', 'ends with' or 'contains'.
Whether LIKE ignores upper/lower case depends on the database, so in answers copy the case given in the question.
core.h: Pattern matching with LIKE and the % wildcard
core.p: **LIKE** is used instead of = when you want to match a **pattern** rather than an exact value. The **%** wildcard stands for **any number of characters (including none)**. So Name LIKE 'S%' finds every name that starts with S, and Name LIKE '%son' finds every name ending in son. It is ideal for searches where only part of the text is known.

bullets: Step 1: read FROM to know which table you are using.
Step 2: apply WHERE to each row; cross out any row where the condition is false.
Step 3: for the surviving rows, write only the fields named in SELECT, in that order.
Check boundaries: does the operator include the exact value (>=, <=) or not (>, <)?
With AND check both conditions; with OR a row needs only one.
Check the **number of records** returned and that you have not missed a matching row lower down the table.
If the question asks 'how many records', count the rows in the result set.
core.h: Reading a query and predicting its output
core.p: A skill that is often examined is looking at a table and a query and writing down exactly what is returned. Work in the same order that SQL does: first find the **table** (FROM), then keep only the **records** that satisfy the **WHERE** condition, and finally show only the **fields** listed in SELECT. Test every single record, one at a time, so you do not miss any. Present the answer as the columns requested, in the order requested.

bullets: Words like 'show', 'list', 'display', 'find the names of' tell you which fields go after SELECT.
Words like 'who', 'where', 'only', 'that have', 'greater than', 'more than' signal the WHERE condition.
'More than 50' means > 50; 'at least 50' means >= 50; 'fewer than' means <; 'at most' means <=.
'Starts with', 'ends with', 'contains' signals LIKE and %.
'Both/and' signals AND; 'either/or' signals OR.
Finally check: SELECT → FROM → WHERE order, commas between fields, quotes round text, spelling of every name.
core.h: Writing a query from a description
core.p: To write a query from scratch, translate the sentence into the three parts: which fields (SELECT), which table (FROM), which records (WHERE). Underline the words in the question that name fields and values, and decide whether each is a column to display or a condition to test. Write the keywords in capitals, check the quotes round text, then reread the question to make sure every part is covered.

bullets: **File handling**: each line of a text/CSV file is often one record, with fields separated by commas.
**Arrays**: a table in memory can be an array of records or a 2D array.
**Validation**: range, type, presence and length checks keep the data in each field sensible.
**Boolean logic**: AND/OR in SQL behave like AND/OR in IF statements and logic gates.
**Cyber security**: **SQL injection** is when an attacker enters SQL code into an input box to read or damage the database; prevented by input sanitisation and validation.
**Data types and casting**: fields are read from files as strings and must be cast to numbers for comparison.
**Testing**: test a query with boundary values (such as exactly 50) to check >, >=, <, <=.
core.p: Records and SQL connect to several other parts of the J277 course, and linking them is a good way to gain evaluation and application marks. They connect to file handling (records are saved and loaded as lines), to arrays (an array of records is a table in memory), to validation (data should be checked before it is stored) and to cyber security (SQL injection attacks target badly protected database queries). Understanding the links helps with longer, applied questions.

exam: 1 mark 'State what is meant by a record': 'A collection of related fields about one entity / one row of a table'. Do not just say 'data'.
1 mark 'What is a field?': 'A single item of data within a record / one column of a table'. Use the words 'single' or 'one item'.
2 mark 'Describe the difference between a record and a field': one mark for each correct definition; link them: a record is made of fields.
Query-reading questions (2 to 4 marks): apply WHERE to every row, then show only the SELECT fields, in the order given. Show your working by crossing out rows.
Query-writing questions (3 to 4 marks): marks are usually for correct SELECT fields, correct FROM table, correct WHERE condition, and correct use of AND/OR/LIKE. Write each clause on its own line.
Command word 'State' / 'Give' = a short fact. 'Describe' = say what happens or what it is in a sentence. 'Explain' = give a reason using 'because' or 'so that'.
Boundary traps: 'over', 'more than', 'above' means >; 'at least', 'minimum' means >=; 'under', 'below' means <; 'at most', 'no more than' means <=.
For 'explain why records are used' write a benefit and a reason: 'Fields about one item are stored together, so the data is organised and easier to search and update'.
For 'explain one benefit of SQL', say it is quicker/easier than writing a program to loop through all records, and the database returns only what is needed.
Always check the table name, the field names and spelling against the question: marks are lost for invented names.
If a query returns nothing, say 'no records' rather than leaving the answer blank, if the question asks what is displayed.

mistakes.r: A record is one row (all the data about one thing); a field is one column (one named item).
mistakes.w: A field is a row and a record is a column.

mistakes.r: SELECT chooses the fields (columns). WHERE chooses which records (rows) meet the condition.
mistakes.w: SELECT is used to choose which records are returned.

mistakes.r: 'At least 50' includes 50, so use Score >= 50. Check the boundary value.
mistakes.w: Writing WHERE Score > 50 when the question says 'at least 50'.

mistakes.r: Text values need quotes: WHERE Name = 'Chloe'. Numbers do not.
mistakes.w: Leaving out quotes round text: WHERE Name = Chloe.

mistakes.r: Repeat the field in each condition: WHERE Score > 40 AND Score < 70.
Use LIKE for patterns: WHERE Name LIKE 'S%'.
mistakes.w: Using = with a wildcard: WHERE Name = 'S%'.

mistakes.r: AND needs both conditions true so returns fewer; OR needs either so returns the same or more.
mistakes.w: Thinking AND returns more records than OR.

mistakes.r: The order is SELECT, FROM, WHERE.
mistakes.w: Putting the clauses in the wrong order (WHERE before FROM).

mistakes.r: An array holds items of the same data type accessed by index; a record holds related fields (possibly different types) accessed by field name.
mistakes.w: Saying an array and a record are the same.

mistakes.r: SQL is a query language: you state what data you want and the database finds it; it does not need a loop written by the programmer.
mistakes.w: SQL is a programming language that runs loops to find data.

summary: The spec asks you to know that data is stored in records made of fields, and to use SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, LIKE, AND, OR) to search for data in a database table. You must be able to read a query and say what it returns, and write one from a description. It matters because databases and file records underpin almost every program that stores information.

terms.d: A collection of related fields that stores data about one entity, such as one student; one row of a table.
A single named item of data within a record; one column of a table, with a name and a data type.
A set of records of the same structure, made up of rows (records) and columns (fields).
A database that stores all of its data in a single table.
The identifier used to refer to a field, such as Name or Score.
The kind of value a field can hold, such as integer, real, string or Boolean.
An array in which each element is a whole record, used to hold a table in memory.
Structured Query Language; a language used to search for and retrieve data from a database.
A request for data from a database, written in a language such as SQL.
The SQL keyword that states which fields (columns) are to be returned.
The SQL keyword that states which table the data is to be taken from.
The SQL keyword that states the condition records must meet to be returned.
In SELECT, means all fields of the table.
The SQL keyword used with a pattern to match text, e.g. Name LIKE 'S%'.
A symbol used in a LIKE pattern that stands for any number of characters, including none.
Combines conditions so that both must be true for a record to be returned.
Combines conditions so that at least one must be true for a record to be returned.
The data returned by a query, containing only the requested fields and matching records.

worked.ans: (a) Amir, Chloe, Ella. (b) SELECT * FROM Students WHERE Year = 11 AND Score > 50  (returns Chloe and Ella).
worked.q:
The table Students has the records below. (a) State the output of: SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Score >= 60. [2]  (b) Write an SQL query to display all fields of Year 11 students with a score above 50. [4]
ID, Name, Year, Score: 1 Amir 10 72; 2 Beth 11 48; 3 Chloe 11 65; 4 Dev 10 39; 5 Ella 11 81; 6 Sam 10 55
steps: (a) Apply WHERE Score >= 60 to every record: Amir 72 yes; Beth 48 no; Chloe 65 yes; Dev 39 no; Ella 81 yes; Sam 55 no.
SELECT Name means only the Name column is displayed.
(b) Fields: all of them, so SELECT *. Table: Students, so FROM Students.
Conditions: Year = 11 AND Score > 50. Both must be true, so use AND. 'Above 50' is >, not >=.
Check against the table: Beth is Year 11 but 48 is not above 50; Chloe (65) and Ella (81) pass.

worked.q: Using the same Students table, give the output of SELECT Name, Score FROM Students WHERE Year = 10 OR Score > 80. [3]
steps: Test each record: Amir Year 10 so included; Beth Year 11 and 48 so no; Chloe Year 11 and 65 so no.
Dev Year 10 so included; Ella Year 11 but 81 > 80 so included; Sam Year 10 so included.
OR means one true condition is enough, so four records are returned.
Show only Name and Score in that order.

worked.ans: SELECT Name, Score FROM Students WHERE Name LIKE 'S%'. LIKE is used because we are matching a pattern (part of the text) rather than an exact value; = would only match the single value 'S%'. Result for the table above: Sam 55.
worked.q: A school stores students in the table Students. Write an SQL query to show the Name and Score of every student whose name begins with the letter S, and explain why LIKE is used instead of =. [4]
steps: Fields requested: Name and Score, so SELECT Name, Score.
Condition: begins with S, so a pattern is needed: Name LIKE 'S%'.
% stands for any characters after the S, so the pattern matches Sam but not Amir.
